---
title: "Estimate immune and stromal cells from a bulk RNA-seq table"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

This page goes from a gene-by-sample TPM table to cell-type scores, and then to a consensus across methods.
To show what comes out, it builds a small synthetic table in which the answer is known: samples S1 to S4 have
six times the expression of T cell marker genes, and S5 to S8 have six times the expression of B cell marker
genes. All output below comes from running the code.

## 1. The table you need

One row per gene symbol, one column per sample, TPM values that are not log-transformed. A data frame (symbols
in the first column) or a numeric matrix (symbols as row names) both work. From RSEM files,
[rsemverse](https://daikikumakura.github.io/rsemverse/) makes exactly this table:

```{r}
tpm <- rsemverse::rsem_read("rsem", "metadata.csv", species = "human", expr = "tpm")
```

Here is the synthetic one:

```{r}
library(bulkdeconv)

markers <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "mcp_counter", "markers.rds", package = "bulkdeconv"))
danaher <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "danaher", "markers.rds", package = "bulkdeconv"))
mcp_T <- markers[["HUGO symbols"]][markers[["Cell population"]] == "T cells"]
mcp_B <- markers[["HUGO symbols"]][markers[["Cell population"]] == "B lineage"]
t_genes <- unique(c(mcp_T, danaher[["T-cells"]]))
b_genes <- unique(c(mcp_B, danaher[["B-cells"]]))

genes <- unique(c(markers[["HUGO symbols"]], unlist(danaher), sprintf("GENE%03d", 1:300)))
set.seed(7)
n <- 8
tpm <- matrix(rlnorm(length(genes) * n, 2, 0.8), length(genes), n,
              dimnames = list(genes, paste0("S", 1:n)))
tpm[t_genes, 1:4] <- tpm[t_genes, 1:4] * 6     # T cell rich
tpm[b_genes, 5:8] <- tpm[b_genes, 5:8] * 6     # B cell rich
tpm <- sweep(tpm, 2, colSums(tpm), "/") * 1e6  # TPM
dim(tpm)
```

```text
[1] 454   8
```

## 2. Choose a method

```{r}
methods <- bulkdeconv_methods()
methods[methods$species %in% c("human", "human|mouse"),
        c("method", "status", "expr_accepted", "min_samples_n", "output_class")]
```

The table lists 25 methods. The columns that matter first:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `ready` runs now. `conditional` needs something more: a cancer type, a tissue, or at least a few samples (see `min_samples_n`). |
| `expr_accepted` | `tpm` for all but `seqimmucc`, which takes counts. |
| `min_samples_n` | The fewest samples the method accepts. |
| `output_class` | What the numbers are: `fraction`, `abundance_score`, `enrichment_score` and so on. |

A fraction (quanTIseq, EPIC) is a share of cells. A score (MCP-counter, xCell) has arbitrary units: it orders
samples for one cell type, and it cannot be compared between cell types. Choose by what you want to say, not by
which method gives the larger numbers.

## 3. Run one method

```{r}
res <- bulkdeconv(tpm, expr = "tpm", species = "human", method = "mcp_counter")
round(res$score[, c("T cells", "B lineage", "CD8 T cells")], 1)
```

```text
   T cells B lineage CD8 T cells
S1 18112.0    1527.7       561.3
S2  9482.9    2754.1      1267.3
S3 10151.9    1765.4      1778.3
S4 13443.7    1398.9      2457.3
S5  1242.4   11681.0      1688.9
S6  2820.8    6488.9      1225.2
S7  2307.1   15813.3       501.9
S8  1726.4   12626.9      1203.3
```

The T cell score is high in S1 to S4 and the B lineage score in S5 to S8, as built. Read down a column, not
across a row: `18112` against `1527.7` in S1 says nothing about more T cells than B cells.

The result says how to read itself:

```{r}
res$metadata$output_class     # "abundance_score"
res$metadata$comparability    # "arbitrary units; comparable across samples for one cell type, not across cell types"
res$qc$signature_genes        # 111 marker genes in the method
res$qc$signature_genes_found  # 111 of them are in your table
```

## 4. Check the coverage

A method can only use the genes your table has. `qc` counts them. Remove six T cell marker genes and run again:

```{r}
part <- tpm[!rownames(tpm) %in% mcp_T[1:6], ]
rp <- bulkdeconv(part, "tpm", "human", "mcp_counter")
rp$qc[c("signature_genes", "signature_genes_found")]
```

```text
$signature_genes
[1] 111

$signature_genes_found
[1] 105
```

Look at this before you trust a score: a method that finds half of its signature genes still returns numbers.

## 5. What the input checks refuse

`bulkdeconv()` stops with a message that says what to change, instead of returning numbers that mean nothing:

| You pass | Message |
|---|---|
| `expr = "count"` to a TPM method | `Method 'mcp_counter' accepts expr = "tpm", not "count". Convert counts to TPM (rsemverse::rsem_read(expr = "tpm")) instead.` |
| log-transformed or negative values | `data` contains negative values (40). Counts and TPM are non-negative; log-transformed or batch-corrected data is not supported. |
| a gene symbol twice | `1 gene symbol(s) occur more than once (e.g. CD28). Merge duplicates before calling bulkdeconv(); ...` |
| mouse symbols as `species = "human"` (or the reverse) | `species` is "mouse" but only 0% of the gene symbols contain lower-case letters; human symbols are upper case (e.g. ACTB). |
| a method whose packages are not installed | `The packages for 'epic' are not installed. Run bulkdeconv_install("epic") first.` |

The last one is the three methods that run from their original packages (EPIC, DCQ, SSMD):
`bulkdeconv_install("epic")` installs them once into a private library, so your own library is untouched.

## 6. Two methods, one consensus

Different methods disagree on the numbers, so a single method is weak evidence. Run a second one, then combine:

```{r}
r2 <- bulkdeconv(tpm, "tpm", "human", "danaher")
round(r2$score[, c("T-cells", "B-cells")], 2)
```

```text
   T-cells B-cells
S1   12.43   10.39
S2   12.78   10.38
S3   12.35   10.93
S4   13.01   10.10
S5   11.01   12.98
S6   10.50   12.50
S7   10.37   13.57
S8    9.96   13.31
```

```{r}
cons <- bulkdeconv_consensus(list(mcp_counter = res, danaher = r2))
round(cons$score, 2)
round(cons$agreement, 2)
```

```text
   B_cell dendritic neutrophil   NK T_CD8
S1   0.25      0.31       0.38 0.44  0.19
S2   0.31      0.38       0.75 0.56  0.50
S3   0.38      0.69       0.56 0.62  0.75
S4   0.06      0.56       0.06 0.88  0.75
S5   0.69      0.19       0.75 0.50  0.81
S6   0.56      0.62       0.75 0.44  0.62
S7   0.94      0.50       0.31 0.50  0.06
S8   0.81      0.75       0.44 0.06  0.31

    B_cell  dendritic neutrophil         NK      T_CD8
      0.93      -0.19       0.33       0.10       0.71
```

The consensus replaces every method's numbers by their percentile rank among the samples, averages the ranks
of the columns of one cell lineage within a method, and then averages across methods
([`?bulkdeconv_consensus`](https://daikikumakura.github.io/bulkdeconv/reference/bulkdeconv_consensus.html)).
So `score` orders the samples within one lineage (the B cell column is highest for S5 to S8); it is not a
fraction, it cannot be compared between lineages, and adding a sample changes every value.

`agreement` is the mean Spearman correlation between the methods that cover the lineage. It is high for B cells
(0.93) and low for dendritic cells (−0.19): in this table nothing was changed for dendritic cell genes, so the
two methods rank random noise differently. A low agreement tells you not to read that column. Which output
columns entered which lineage is in `cons$sources`, and what was left out and why is in `cons$dropped`: here,
endothelial, fibroblast, macrophage and monocyte were each covered by only one method, and the consensus
needs two.

## 7. Next

- `bulkdeconv_methods()` shows the licence and version of each method, and `bulkdeconv_lineages()` how output
  columns map to lineages.
- Methods with a minimum sample count (`min_samples_n`), or a cancer type (`cancer_type = ` for TIMER), are
  explained in `?bulkdeconv`.
- [Sources and licences of the methods](https://github.com/DaikiKumakura/bulkdeconv/blob/main/inst/COPYRIGHTS).
